title: A Gallery of Systems
intro: Every system in the two viewers, one after another: what each picture shows, the poles as the readout prints them, what to try, and the one thing each system teaches. Ten live in the plane and six in space.

blocks.text: How to use this page

Every entry below is a full viewer, set to one preset, so you can leave it on this page and experiment: nothing you do to one viewer affects the others. All the two-state viewers have the same controls (System, Time, Sample period T (seconds), Input, x₁(0), x₂(0), Feedback gain k₁ and k₂) and the three-state ones have System, Input, x₁(0), x₂(0), x₃(0), Turn and Tilt. Changing System resets the feedback gains to 0. The gallery's choice of system is only a starting point, and Next step ▶ walks through the eight steps for whatever is selected. Where an entry says 'the readout shows', the text in quotes is what the line under that viewer prints at the preset settings.

The numbers are worked out on the pages States and the State Equations (#/math/state-space/state-equations), Solving the State Equations (#/math/state-space/solving), Modes and Stability (#/math/state-space/modes-and-stability), Transfer Functions and Realisations (#/math/state-space/transfer-functions), Sampled and Discrete-Time Systems (#/math/state-space/discrete-time), Controllability and Observability (#/math/state-space/controllability-observability), State Feedback and Pole Placement (#/math/state-space/state-feedback) and Three States and More (#/math/state-space/higher-order); the formulas are collected on State-Space Tables (#/math/state-space/tables). Ten systems have two states and six have three.
Mechanical and electrical
Mass on a spring, light damping

widget.title: Mass on a spring, light damping

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one
params.default: mass on a spring, light damping

blocks.text: A 1 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 4 N/m with damping 1 N·s/m, pushed by a force $u$. The poles are $-0.5 \pm 1.936j$, which is a natural frequency of 2 rad/s and a damping ratio of 0.25. Here the force is a unit step and the mass starts at rest: the dark path starts at the origin and spirals to the red + marked 'rest' at $(0.25, 0)$, where the spring force $4x_1$ balances the push. The output overshoots to 0.361 at 1.6 s, 44% above its final value, because so little damping is present.

Drag Feedback gain k₁ to 4 and k₂ to 3. The readout shows 'Feedback K = (4.0, 3.0): A − BK = [[0, 1], [−8, −4]]. Poles −2 ± 2j: stable.' and the + jumps to $(0.125, 0)$: feedback made the spring stiffer (8 instead of 4) and added damping, but also halved the steady-state gain. It teaches what feedback does to poles, and what it costs.
Mass on a spring, heavy damping

widget.title: Mass on a spring, heavy damping

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one
params.default: mass on a spring, heavy damping

blocks.text: A unit mass on a softer spring, stiffness 2, with damping 3: $G = 1/(s^2 + 3s + 2)$ and real poles $-1$ and $-2$. The two dashed lines are the eigen-directions, labelled 'λ = −1' and 'λ = −2'. From $x(0) = (1, 0)$ the path does not spiral: the fast mode dies first, so the path moves across (parallel to the $\lambda = -2$ line) onto the slow $\lambda = -1$ line, then slides in along it, and the position never crosses zero. The speed $x_2$ dips to $-0.5$ at 0.69 s and returns.

Set x₂(0) to −1: now the start sits on the $\lambda = -1$ line and the state moves straight in, decaying like $e^{-t}$ (the readout ends 'At t = 5 s: x = (0.01, −0.01), y = 0.007'). Set x₂(0) to −2 and it rides the $\lambda = -2$ line, twice as fast. It teaches that a start on an eigen-line is a single mode, and that the slow mode wins in the end.
RLC circuit

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one

blocks.text: A series circuit with $R = 2\ \Omega$, $L = 1$ H and $C = 0.5$ F, driven by a source voltage. The states are the capacitor voltage $x_1$ and the inductor current $x_2$, and the output is $x_1$. The poles are $-1 \pm 1j$, $G = 2/(s^2 + 2s + 2)$, and $G(0) = 1$: the capacitor ends at the source voltage, with no current. The red + sits at $(1, 0)$. The damping ratio is $1/\sqrt{2} = 0.707$, so there is a small overshoot: the output peaks at 1.043 at 3.14 s, which is $\pi$ s, and $1 + e^{-\pi} = 1.043$.

Switch Input to unit impulse (and leave the start at 0): the state jumps by $B = (0, 1)$, the inductor current jumps to 1, and the output is the impulse response $2e^{-t}\sin t$, which peaks at 0.645 at $t = \pi/4 = 0.79$ s. It teaches that the same poles produce the step and impulse responses, and where the 0.707 comes from.
Undamped oscillator

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one

blocks.text: A mass on a spring with no damping at all: $x_1' = x_2$, $x_2' = -x_1$. The poles are $\pm j$, on the imaginary axis, and the readout says 'on the edge'. From $(1, 0)$ the state goes round a circle once every $2\pi = 6.28$ s and the plot spans three turns, 18.85 s, so the readout ends at the start: 'x = (1.00, 0.00), y = 1.000'. There are no dashed lines because the eigenvalues are complex, and no spiral because there is no decay.

Set Time to sampled every T seconds and T to 1.5: the path becomes a ring of dots, each one a turn of 85.9° round the circle. The readout shows 'Poles 0.071 ± 0.997j: on the edge', and the poles sit exactly on the unit circle in the z-plane. It teaches that stability's boundary is the imaginary axis in continuous time and the unit circle when sampled.
Tanks and motors
Two tanks in a row

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one

blocks.text: Water flows into tank 1, tank 1 drains into tank 2, and tank 2 drains out; the output is the level in tank 2. The poles are $-1$ and $-0.5$ (the drain rates), $G = 1/(s^2 + 1.5s + 0.5)$ and the steady-state gain is $G(0) = 2$. With a unit step of inflow the red + sits at $(1, 2)$: tank 1 settles where its drain of $1 \times x_1$ matches the inflow, and tank 2 where $0.5 x_2 = x_1$. There is no spiral, since the poles are real: the path curves in to the + tangent to the slow dashed line, labelled 'λ = −0.5'. The readout ends 'y = 1.973'.

Set Input to none and x₁(0) to 1: tank 1 holds water and tank 2 is empty. The amber curve $x_2$ rises to 0.5 at $t = 2\ln 2 = 1.39$ s and falls: the water passes through. It teaches a system that cannot oscillate, because water cannot flow back, and the steady-state gain as one over the last tank's drain rate, $1/0.5 = 2$.
DC motor, angle and speed

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one

blocks.text: A motor that turns a load: the state is the angle $x_1$ and speed $x_2$, the input is the voltage. The poles are $0$ and $-2$, $G = 2/(s^2 + 2s)$, and the readout says 'on the edge': the pole at 0 is an integrator, since the angle is the integral of the speed. Every point on the $x_1$ axis is a resting point (a motor can stop at any angle). Started with speed 1 at angle 0, the state moves along a straight line in the direction of the $\lambda = -2$ dashed line, and ends at $(0.5, 0)$: the readout ends 'x = (0.50, 0.00), y = 0.500'. The speed 1 is worth an angle of $1/2$ before friction stops it.

Set Input to unit step and x₂(0) back to 0. There is no red +: with a constant voltage the speed settles at 1 but the angle grows without limit, and the readout ends 'x = (7.50, 1.00), y = 7.500'. It teaches what a pole at zero means: no steady state for a step, and an angle that depends on the whole history.
Unstable systems
Pendulum balanced upright

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one

blocks.text: A pendulum linearised about its upright position, with $g/L = 1$: $x_1' = x_2$ and $x_2' = x_1 + u$, so a small tilt makes gravity push it further over. The poles are $+1$ and $-1$, the transfer function $1/(s^2 - 1)$, and the readout says 'unstable'. The plot stops when the motion has grown thirty-fold, at 3.4 s, where it shows 'x = (15.02, 14.98)': the state has been flung out along the unstable line $x_2 = x_1$. This is a saddle: one direction in, one direction out.

Set x₂(0) to −1: the start is on the stable line $\lambda = -1$ and the state falls to $(0.03, -0.03)$ at 3.4 s, a balance that only works for an exact start. Move x₂(0) to −0.9 and it peels away. Then drag k₁ to 3 and k₂ to 2: the readout shows 'Poles −1 ± 1j: stable'. Set k₂ back to 0 and the poles are 'on the edge', ±1.414j. It teaches why an unstable system needs feedback, and that position feedback alone gives no damping.
Negative damping, a growing swing

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one

blocks.text: A mass on a spring whose damping is negative, $x_2' = -x_1 + 0.3x_2$: it pushes the motion instead of resisting it. The poles are $0.15 \pm 0.989j$, in the right half of the s-plane (the shaded part), so the path is a spiral that opens outwards. It swings about once every 6.4 s and each swing is about $e^{0.15 \times 6.35} = 2.6$ times the last. The plot spans 20 s and ends at 'x = (9.67, −16.21)'.

Drag Feedback gain k₂ up from 0. At 0.3 the readout shows 'Poles ±1j: on the edge' and the path closes into a circle; at 0.6 it shows 'Poles −0.15 ± 0.989j: stable' and the spiral turns inwards. The trace of the closed-loop matrix, $0.3 - k_2$, is the sum of the poles' real parts. It teaches that a complex pair's stability is decided by the sign of its real part, which for a 2×2 matrix is half the trace.
Hidden modes
Hidden mode: the input misses one

widget.title: Hidden mode: the input misses one

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one
params.default: hidden mode: the input misses one

blocks.text: Two independent first-order modes, with $A = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -2)$ and the input entering only the first, $B = (1, 0)$. The output adds the two states, $C = (1, 1)$. The poles are $-1$ and $-2$, but the transfer function the readout prints is $(s + 2)/(s^2 + 3s + 2)$, which simplifies to $1/(s + 1)$: the pole at $-2$ is cancelled by a zero. The readout says 'Not controllable, observable'. In the plane the input pushes only along $x_1$, so the + sits at $(1, 0)$, and the amber $x_2$ simply dies away like $e^{-2t}$ from its start of 1, whatever the input does.

Set Feedback gain k₁ to 2: the readout shows 'Feedback K = (2.0, 0.0): A − BK = [[−3, 0], [0, −2]]. Poles −2 and −3'. The pole at $-1$ moved to $-3$ but the one at $-2$ stayed, however you set k₁ and k₂ (k₂ only changes an off-diagonal entry of $A - BK$ and moves no pole). It teaches that a mode the input cannot reach cannot be moved either.
Hidden mode: the output misses one

widget.title: Hidden mode: the output misses one

params.label: System
options: mass on a spring, light damping
mass on a spring, heavy damping
hidden mode: the input misses one
hidden mode: the output misses one
params.default: hidden mode: the output misses one

blocks.text: The mirror image: $A = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -2)$ again, but now the input drives both states, $B = (1, 1)$, and the output sees only the first, $C = (1, 0)$. The transfer function is the same, $(s + 2)/(s^2 + 3s + 2) = 1/(s + 1)$, but the readout says 'Controllable, not observable'. The state really moves in both directions: the red + sits at $(1, 0.5)$ and the amber curve $x_2$ rises to 0.5, but the thick red $y$ follows $x_1$ alone and never shows it. From outside, the system looks first order.

Set k₁ to 5 and k₂ to −4: both poles can be moved, to $-2 \pm 2j$ (the readout says 'Poles −2 ± 2j: stable'), because the input reaches both modes. The zero at $-2$ stays: 'G(s) = (s + 2) / (s² + 4s + 8)'. It teaches that a hidden mode is a fact about the output, not the input, and that feedback does not move zeros.
Three states
Spring with a slow actuator

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: A spring like the first entry's ($m = 1$, $k = 4$) but with less damping, $c = 0.4$, and driven through an actuator with a 0.2 s lag. The poles are $-0.2 \pm 1.99j$ and $-5$, and $G = 5/(s^3 + 5.4s^2 + 6s + 20)$. With a unit step from rest the red + sits at $(0.25, 0, 1)$: the actuator force settles at the command 1 and the spring at $1/4$. The output rises to a peak of about 0.42 near 1.8 s, then rings down to 0.25: the readout ends 'x = (0.25, 0.00, 1.00), y = 0.249'. The slow actuator only shows in the first second, in the violet curve $x_3$ climbing to 1.

Set Tilt to 85 to look down on the floor: the faint shadow of the path is a spiral round $(0.25, 0)$, much like the two-state spring's picture. It teaches the dominant poles: the response is almost the second-order one, with a small delay from the third pole.
DC motor with its current

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: A DC motor like the one in the last section, now with its electrical side included (its numbers differ): the angle, the speed and the current. The poles are $0$, $-1.219$ and $-3.281$, $G = 2/(s^3 + 4.5s^2 + 4s)$, and the readout says 'on the edge'. The three eigen-directions are dashed; the one for $\lambda = 0$ is the $x_1$ axis, along which every point is a resting point. Starting with speed 1, angle and current 0, the path curves round and ends on the axis at $x_1 = 1$, which is the readout's 'x = (1.00, 0.00, 0.00), y = 1.000'. That is the left-eigenvector rule: the final angle is $x_1 + x_2 + 0.25x_3$ of the start.

Set x₃(0) to 2 and the readout ends at $x_1 = 0 + 1 + 0.25 \times 2 = 1.5$. Set Input to unit step with x(0) = 0: no resting point and no +, and the angle ramps. It teaches that an integrator makes the final position depend on the start, and how to find it with one dot product.
Three tanks in a row

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: Three tanks in a row with drain rates 1, 0.6 and 0.3; the output is tank 3. The poles are all real, $-1$, $-0.6$ and $-0.3$, and $G = 0.6/(s^3 + 1.9s^2 + 1.08s + 0.18)$. Start with tank 1 holding 2 and the others empty: the water moves down the cascade. Tank 2 peaks at 0.93 near 1.3 s, tank 3 at 0.90 near 3.5 s, and then everything drains away along the slowest mode, $e^{-0.3t}$ (tank 3 ends at 0.04: the readout shows 'x = (0.00, 0.00, 0.04), y = 0.038' at 16.67 s). The three dashed eigen-lines are straight, and the path curves between them.

Set Input to unit step with x(0) = 0 instead: the + sits at $(1, 1.67, 3.33)$ and the level in tank 3 follows an S-shaped curve with no overshoot. It teaches that three real poles make a path that never spirals, and that the slowest drain sets the settling time: the viewer's rule of thumb gives $4/0.3 = 13.3$ s, and the two faster lags add a delay that stretches it to about 16.5 s.
Chain of three lags

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: The system $1/(s + 1)^3$ in companion form: $x_2 = x_1'$, $x_3 = x_1''$. The triple pole is $-1$ and the matrix is defective, so there is only one dashed line, 'λ = −1'. With a unit impulse at rest, the state jumps by $B = (0, 0, 1)$ (the short dashed red segment) and the output is the impulse response $\tfrac12 t^2e^{-t}$: zero at first, then a hump of height 0.271 at $t = 2$ s, then a tail. The hump is the polynomial factor $t^2$ fighting $e^{-t}$.

Switch Input to none and set x₃(0) to 1: the same state, now simply started there instead of kicked, gives the same curves. The readout ends 'At t = 11 s: x = (0.00, 0.00, 0.00), y = 0.001'. It teaches that an impulse is just a very short push, equivalent to starting at $B$, and what a repeated pole costs: a hump and a slow tail instead of a clean decay.
A spin about an axis, and a decay

widget.title: A spin about an axis, and a decay

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay
params.default: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: Rotation in the first two states ($\pm j$) and a decay in the third ($-0.5$). With the Tilt at 80 you look almost straight down on the amber disc, and with a unit step from rest the path is a circle round the resting point $(0, 1, 2)$, drawn as a red +, while the state climbs to $x_3 = 2$. The readout says 'Poles ±1j and −0.5: on the edge', and ends 'x = (0.00, 0.00, 2.00), y = 2.000' after exactly three turns at 18.85 s. The zeros are $-0.125 \pm 0.696j$.

Set Tilt to 10 and the circle flattens into an ellipse seen edge-on, while the lift in $x_3$ shows clearly. Set Input to none and x(0) to $(1, 0, 1)$: the circle is centred on the origin and it is the height that decays. It teaches a centre in a plane, which neither grows nor decays, joined to a decay along the axis.
Lorenz system near the origin

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: The linearised Lorenz system, a saddle: poles $11.828$, $-2.667$ and $-22.828$, one growing and two decaying, and 'unstable'. It is neither controllable nor observable, because $z$ is decoupled from $x$ and $y$, and the readout says so. The state shoots out along the line with $\lambda = 11.828$, which has slope 2.18 in the $x$–$y$ plane. The plot lasts only 0.29 s, the time for thirty-fold growth, and from this small start, $(0.1, 0, 0.1)$, it ends at 'x = (1.11, 2.42, 0.05), y = 1.111'.

Compare with the default start $(1, 0, 1)$, which ends at ten times the size, $(11.11, 24.24, 0.46)$: a linear system scales, so ten times the start is ten times the end. In the real Lorenz system the nonlinear terms stop this growth. The linear model is only valid while the state is small, here for a fraction of a second. It teaches what 'near the origin' means, and why a linear model is only a local one.
